hero_deck: AccreditaPass tells a reporter covering the 2026 World Cup what their press pass allows, before a gate turns them away.
hero_rv_txt: Picture 104 matches in 16 stadiums across three countries, with every press pass still moving after it is issued. A venue swaps, a zone narrows, a knockout seat waits on a result nobody has played. Without a record, the holder finds out at a turnstile. AccreditaPass keeps one record per journalist that says what changed, why, and what to do next. I audited, researched, specified and built it in five weeks, as a portfolio demonstration rather than a product.
badge_independence_body: Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to FIFA. All accreditation data is simulated for the browser session and nothing is persisted. The match schedule is the one real thing in it.
badge_simulated_body: No human participants took part in any study on this page: every dataset, workshop participant and task-attempt was authored, not recruited.
act2_question: How might we tell a journalist that their access has changed before they discover it by being refused?
act5_footnote: First audit measured the pre-reframing app at commit 0653b4e. Re-audit measured the build at b37066d. Both used simulated task-attempts and authored participants; neither involved a human user.
hero_role3: Scope — Audit → research → specification → build → re-audit
act1_lede: The holder is the last to know.
act2_verdict: No journalist was interviewed. The study says so.
act2_lede: Three passes before the record was built.
p1_x: A press pass resolves to venues, zones and fixtures, and any of them can change after it is issued.
p1_r: Rejection, a mid-tournament reallocation and a denial at the gate are three different events with one experience: the holder learns last, often at the gate itself.
p2_x: A page that shows what you hold today answers the wrong question.
p2_r: A holder needs what changed, when, why and what to do next — a history with reasons, not a snapshot.
p3_x: Access to a knockout fixture depends on a result nobody has played yet.
p3_r: Wording that sounds settled turns a warning into a promise the service cannot keep, so every conditional right is written as a condition.
p4_x: My own course app returned 26 audit findings, 4 of them critical.
p4_r: Most traced back to one component that could only be edited, reused on every page. Every finding cites its file and line, and the fix list ran to 19 commits.
l1_x: A 30-respondent survey and five interviews, both synthetic, produced two personas and a service blueprint.
l2_x: Six authored participants argued 32 ideas down to a shortlist of eight, then to one: Access Record.
l3_x: Nine gates fixed the information architecture, WCAG 2.2 AA tokens and the build brief before any interface code.
sch_verdict: Five weeks, and the research went first.
sch_lede: Every bar comes from the commit history.
sch_note: Reconstructed from the public commit history of github.com/jdsaire/accreditapass: 206 commits across 16 runs, 28 Jul – 30 Aug 2026. The research, ideation and specification dossiers were written outside the repository, so their bars mark the day each one entered it. Nothing was committed from 1 to 10 August or from 21 to 28 August.
gantt_noscript: This chart draws from its data with JavaScript. Every window it shows is also stated in the note below.
gt_v3: Usability and accessibility audit, then fixes
act4_verdict: Built to say what it is.
act5_verdict: Measured twice, on the same instruments.
act5_lede: The re-audit ran against the shipped build.
ev_disposition: All 26 first-audit findings got a disposition: 18 fixed, 5 not applicable, 2 open and 1 partly fixed.
ev_tests: 512 front-end and 33 back-end automated tests, in xUnit and bUnit.
b1_x: A Blazor WebAssembly client runs on an in-memory mock, so the live site works with no server behind it.
b1_r: An ASP.NET Core Web API ships in the repository, switched off by default. When it runs, SignalR pushes each new change to the open record.
b2_x: English, Spanish and Portuguese carry 339 entries each, at exact parity.
b2_r: Language and theme are independent of each other and of the session, so changing either never signs you out.
b3_x: The sign-in prints its own passwords, and the API token is a fixed string in the repository.
b3_r: Neither secures anything, and both say so wherever a reader could mistake them for real. A fixture that has not been played never names its teams, in any language.
b4_x: Seven routes, and the record is gated because an access record is personal.
b4_r: Requesting access writes a new entry to your record instead of showing a separate confirmation screen. The schedule and the help page stay public.
act6_verdict: What this build lets me say.
r1_x: I completed Back-End Development with .NET, and its capstone shipped as its own repository.
r2_x: I set Full-Stack Integration aside, and every study on this page ran on simulated participants.
r3_x: I am learning front-to-back integration, and a second part of this series will show it before 2026 closes.
sim_c1_x: A payment-verification flow rebuilt as an operator-legible sequence.
sim_c2_x: The system this brief is published on — built, governed, and operated end to end.
